bridges.mechanism: An increase in crude prices directly raises expected near-term energy and transport costs, leading firms and households to revise up short- and medium-term inflation expectations.

Sustained spikes in global oil prices boost export revenue for Russia on short notice, increasing available budget and hard-currency purchasing power to procure, field, or replenish drones and munitions, thereby raising the frequency of drone attacks in the Ukraine theater.

Sharp rises in global oil prices raise production and transport costs and short‑term inflation, prompting risk‑off reallocations and reducing cross‑border equity and project finance into Taiwan's manufacturing and tech sectors.

Elevated oil prices increase fiscal and liquidity cushions for Gulf sovereign funds and exporters, prompting accelerated outbound strategic investments and acquisitions into global tech and industrial assets that affect cross‑border capital flows in the US‑China tech competition.

Sustained reductions in delivered oil to regional markets raise energy scarcity and costs and can force energy‑intensive advanced manufacturing (e.g., fabs, chemical precursors) to curtail output, lowering operable production capacity.

Higher chokepoint transit volumes raise immediate FX receipts for oil-exporting economies (and reduce payment-side volatility for importers), supporting those exporters' currencies and putting upward pressure on their exchange-rate levels versus major currencies.

A drop in tanker and general-cargo transit through critical chokepoints constrains global shipping capacity, raises freight and insurance costs, and produces port delays that directly delay or reduce imports of commercially‑sourced drone components into the Russia–Ukraine supply ecosystem.

A rise in maritime incidents forces urgent rerouting, increases trade/disruption-related margin calls and insurance collateral for shippers and commodity traders, and spikes short-term demand for dollar trade and pre-export finance, widening cross-currency basis spreads and funding stress.

A rising rate of hostile or interdiction incidents in key sea lanes immediately raises transit delays, carrier cancellations and insurance costs, forcing Taiwanese exporters to cut shipment volumes and cadence.

Increased maritime disruptions delay or cancel shipment of specialized equipment and parts and discourage on‑site transfers and joint engineering visits, directly slowing cross‑border movement of technical know‑how and hardware.

A sustained rise in hostile or interdiction incidents in the Hormuz corridor triggers tighter licensing, sanctions enforcement and precautionary export-controls by the US and partners on shipments and dual‑use technologies transiting the region.

More frequent attacks, seizures and interdictions cause immediate port delays, re‑routing, ship detentions and insurance refusals that degrade firms' ability to maintain timely component and material flows across tech value chains.

A jump in the oil market risk premium increases FX volatility and triggers sudden capital flow swings (flight-to-safety or rapid outflows from commodity-linked currencies), prompting central banks to conduct more frequent or larger FX interventions to limit disorderly moves.

Operational lessons and tactics from intensified drone use in Ukraine are adapted by Gulf-state proxies and militias (and supplied by intermediaries), raising the frequency of drone-enabled harassment and strikes against commercial shipping in the Hormuz area.

Spikes in cross‑border strikes and airspace violations produce abrupt regional capital flows and exchange-rate pressure that prompt central banks and sovereigns to step up deliberate FX operations to stabilise markets.

An uptick in cross‑border strikes and airspace violations in the Russia–Ukraine system elevates global geopolitical tensions and market perceptions of contagion risk, causing traders to add a higher security/risk premium to oil tied to Hormuz-route vulnerabilities.

An uptick in cross‑border strikes and airspace violations in Ukraine raises perceived geopolitical risk among global investors, causing near‑term reductions or repricing of capital flows into technology and manufacturing assets tied to Taiwan/China.

An uptick in cross‑border strikes, airspace violations or spillovers raises geopolitical risk perceptions and prompts investors and financiers to reduce or delay cross‑border FDI and portfolio flows into sensitive tech sectors.

Rising operational/political pressure to prevent rapid military technology transfer observed in the Russia–Ukraine war prompts governments to expand export controls and licensing on dual‑use and advanced technologies that affect cross‑strait trade policy.

Rising political and operational pressure increases policymakers' appetite to impose broader and stricter export controls and licensing on dual‑use and strategic technologies between the US and China.

Shortages of key electronic and mechanical components force firms and banks to draw additional dollar/foreign-currency working capital and hedges, increasing demand for cross-currency funding and widening basis spreads.

War-driven shortages and export bottlenecks for specialty inputs (e.g., neon, sensors, optics) reduce supply to Taiwanese fabs and R&D lines, slowing chip production upgrades and high-end tech projects.
Interruptions to shipments of energy and grains raise spot and forward commodity prices and expected pass-through to consumer prices, lifting market and survey inflation expectations within weeks.

Sanctions on Russian oil and disruption of Black Sea exports force buyers (especially in Europe and Asia) to source more crude from Middle Eastern producers, increasing tanker departures and transits through the Strait of Hormuz.

Black Sea shipping disruptions, higher freight rates and insurance premia raised by the conflict increase costs and delays for global logistics, directly lowering the volume and timeliness of Taiwan's outbound manufactured shipments.

Shipping bottlenecks, port closures and sanctions interrupt exports and transits of ores, specialty gases and precursor chemicals, directly reducing accessible stocks and imports of critical materials.

Persistent interruptions to routes, longer transit times and increased losses strain inventory buffers and logistics redundancy, directly degrading the ability of high‑tech supply chains to maintain flows and recover.

New or expanded advanced-manufacturing capacity in competing Chinese or allied jurisdictions increases global supply and diverts customer orders away from Taiwanese producers, lowering Taiwan's manufactured export volumes over the following production cycles.

Reduced availability of critical inputs lifts producer costs and supply‑side price pressures in manufacturing chains, which markets and surveys quickly translate into higher expected future consumer inflation (and conversely greater availability lowers those expectations).

Tighter export controls and licensing regimes interrupt normal cross-border payments and correspondent-banking relationships and force firms to seek hard-currency pre-funding or alternative corridors, immediately widening basis spreads and reducing FX liquidity.

Sharp, policy-driven trade restrictions create abrupt one-sided FX flows and volatility (eg sudden export/import payment shifts or sanction-triggered flows), prompting monetary authorities to conduct larger or more frequent FX market interventions to stabilize exchange rates.

Rapid expansion of export controls on maritime and dual‑use technology prompts Beijing to respond with more assertive naval/coast‑guard patrols and closer operational coordination with regional partners (including proxy harassment), increasing hostile interdiction and harassment incidents in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

Broader export controls and tightened secondary‑sanctions enforcement raise legal, compliance and insurance risks for shipowners and charterers, causing firms to suspend or reroute tanker transits through Hormuz and temporarily reduce throughput.

Escalating export controls and visible tech‑rivalry confrontations increase market expectations of retaliatory measures or escalation affecting Gulf transit, so traders and risk‑models add a higher geopolitical risk premium to oil prices.

Tighter export controls and licensing on chips, sensors and dual‑use subsystems directly block legal shipments and raise prices/uncertainty for intermediaries supplying the Russia‑Ukraine theatre, reducing the market availability of drone components within weeks.

Stricter export controls incentivize covert routing and use of third‑country brokers for restricted tech transfers, increasing the number of interdictions, seizures and contested transit incidents that cross political or physical borders.

Tighter export controls and licensing (e.g., US/Allied restrictions on chip tools and design IP) impose legal and commercial barriers that directly reduce the legal rate at which Taiwanese firms can transfer advanced designs, tooling, and IP to mainland Chinese partners.

Sustained net inflows into a jurisdiction's tech/industrial sectors relax external financing constraints and currency pressure, reducing the need for monetary authorities to hike policy rates (or allowing them to cut) to stabilize markets and fund the economy.

Increased cross‑border capital into relevant manufacturers or trading intermediaries enables ramped production or bulk purchases of complete UAVs and rapid export to combat actors, raising the frequency of drone strikes as inventories and production are expanded.

A fall in cross-border capital (driven by sanctions, tighter screening, or risk aversion tied to the rivalry) immediately reduces net inbound equity and direct investment from Chinese and third‑party investors into Taiwanese industrial and tech firms.

Improved supply‑chain resilience (alternative qualified suppliers, validated second‑source production and logistics redundancies) directly sustains flows of drone parts and spares into combat zones despite sanctions or interdictions, increasing component availability quickly.

Improved resilience (diversified suppliers, redundant logistics, stockpiles) reduces production interruptions and loss of engineering staff, thereby preserving and modestly enhancing Taiwan's cumulative high‑end technical know‑how and production capability.

Increases in Taiwan's high-end semiconductor and sensor production capacity directly raise the global supply of chips and guidance components that are re‑exported or incorporated into drones used by actors in the Russia–Ukraine theater.

When Taiwanese firms (e.g., leading foundries) increase process-node know‑how and deploy it in existing fabs, they directly raise operable advanced-manufacturing throughput (semiconductor wafer starts and advanced module output) available to global markets.

A sustained rise in Taiwan's manufacturing export shipments increases foreign‑currency (USD) inflows into the region, easing demand for safe‑haven currencies and putting downward pressure on major USD bilateral exchange rates (i.e., USD weakens vs affected Asian currencies).

A sudden fall in Taiwan-origin manufactured exports signals weaker global industrial activity and reduces near-term refinery feedstock and refined-product demand, producing fewer tanker loadings and a measurable drop in transit volume through key chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz.

Sustained high-volume outbound shipments of critical components (chips, modules) from Taiwanese manufacturers directly reduce upstream shortages and bottlenecks, thereby improving the ability of US/China technology value chains to maintain production and recover from disruptions.

An increase in cross‑border technology transfer reduces operational uncertainty for multinationals in supply chains, decreasing precautionary drawdowns of USD credit lines and hedging demand and thereby easing cross‑currency funding strains over time.

Accelerated transfer of guidance algorithms, AI payload designs, or manufacturing know‑how from Taiwan to firms in the region enables faster fielding of more effective UAVs by third parties or beneficiaries, raising the frequency and effectiveness of drone attacks in the Russia–Ukraine war.

An uptick in transfers of sensitive designs, process IP or equipment from Taiwanese entities to PRC firms triggers immediate policy responses (licensing changes, new entity listings and stricter export controls) from the US and allies to block further leakage.

An abrupt increase in export controls or licensing on Taiwan tech and components forces corporates and suppliers to pre-fund imports and roll or extend USD hedges, sharply raising demand for dollar liquidity and widening cross‑currency basis spreads.

Escalation of export controls on Taiwanese tech provokes PRC coercive signaling and forward naval/paramilitary deployments as deterrence and bargaining leverage, which increases harassment, interdiction attempts and close encounters by forces operating in distant but politically salient sea lanes including the Strait of Hormuz.

Tighter export controls or licensing restrictions on Taiwanese-origin advanced components and related tooling reduce the channels through which those parts reach intermediaries and end users, lowering the pool of drone components available to participants in the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

Larger net inbound investment capital into Taiwan reduces bilateral capital‑flight and depreciation pressure on regional currencies, lowering the frequency and scale of official FX intervention by regional central banks seeking to defend exchange rates.

Increased cross‑border investment into Taiwanese and regional subcontractors expands manufacturing capacity and inventories for drone subsystems, which after lead times become available to global markets that can supply the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

Increases in cross‑border investment originating in or routed through Taiwanese firms (e.g., project finance, JV capital for fabs abroad) directly raise measurable cross‑border capital flows into PRC or regional technology sectors involved in the US–China rivalry.

Rising inflation expectations increase macroeconomic and policy uncertainty and boost hedging and precautionary demand, prompting market participants to price a larger geopolitical/supply risk component into oil (higher oil risk premium).
Tighter policy interest rates in major economies raise borrowing costs and damp aggregate demand and commodity financing, reducing near‑term oil consumption and lowering spot crude prices.

Higher global policy interest rates increase home‑market returns and discount rates while raising borrowing costs for leveraged cross‑border deals, directly reducing appetite and feasibility for foreign portfolio and direct investment into Taiwanese industry and tech.

Sustained increases in major policy rates raise global borrowing costs and compress venture and project returns, prompting investors and banks to scale back cross‑border financing for capital‑intensive advanced‑manufacturing and semiconductor investments linked to US–China competition.

Frequent or large official FX interventions are often accompanied by tighter FX monitoring and controls (capital‑flow management) that directly complicate cross‑border payments, royalties and joint‑venture funding, prompting firms to scale back or slow formal technology licensing and co‑development agreements with Taiwanese partners.

Large or highly visible official FX interventions (e.g., persistent currency defense or managed depreciation) are perceived as competitive economic measures and tend to trigger reciprocal political and regulatory responses, including tighter export controls and licensing on sensitive technologies.

A materially stronger reserve currency (e.g., USD) increases the real purchasing power of US/allied defence and security budgets for forward deployments and escorts, sustaining patrol presence in the Strait and lowering the frequency of hostile or interdiction incidents.

A depreciation of the ruble (a rise in the ruble‑per‑USD exchange rate) raises the local currency price of imported drone parts, reducing procurement volumes and diversity of foreign suppliers for components.

A stronger foreign currency (e.g., USD appreciation / higher USD/TWD exchange rate) makes Taiwan's USD‑priced manufactured goods cheaper for buyers abroad, directly raising export volumes as exporters win or expand orders and pass through price competitiveness.

Sharp adverse moves in bilateral exchange rates (an importer’s currency weakening) raise the local‑currency cost of imported critical minerals and precursors, causing buyers to curtail orders and suppliers to reallocate stock, reducing near‑term availability for high‑tech manufacturing.

Acute cross‑currency funding stress raises dollar/working‑capital costs for shipowners, charterers and insurers, causing cancellations, delays or rerouting of tanker voyages and thereby reducing tanker transit volumes through Hormuz.

Rising cross‑currency funding stress increases the cost and reduces the availability of foreign‑currency payments for Russian importers and third‑party intermediaries, choking off purchases of foreign drone components and subsystems.

Elevated cross‑currency funding stress raises the cost and availability constraints of dollar and other foreign funding for Taiwanese firms and foreign investors, causing immediate reductions or delays in cross‑border equity, debt and project finance into Taiwan.

Spikes in cross‑currency funding stress raise hedging costs and cut dollar liquidity for overseas borrowers and investors, forcing suspension or cancellation of FDI, portfolio flows and project financing into tech and industrial projects tied to the US–China rivalry.

nodes.label: Hormuz Standoff: Iran, Oil Markets and Geopolitical Repricing
Global crude oil price
nodes.description: Current market price level of benchmark crude oil expressed as a continuous index (reflecting spot and near-term contract prices).

nodes.label: Physical oil supply rate
nodes.description: Net flow rate of physical crude oil reaching global markets (gross production minus operational outages and embargo-related stoppages) measured per unit time.

nodes.label: Spare production capacity
nodes.description: Available unused upstream production capacity that can be brought online within a short notice window, measured in barrels per day equivalent.

nodes.label: Emergency oil reserve volume
nodes.description: Aggregate quantity of government-held emergency petroleum reserves available for strategic release, measured in barrels.

nodes.label: Chokepoint transit volume
nodes.description: Rate of oil and petroleum tanker cargo transiting critical maritime chokepoints measured in barrels per day or number of transits per period.

nodes.label: Maritime security incident rate
nodes.description: Frequency per unit time of hostile, interdiction, or disruption events affecting commercial shipping in key sea lanes.

nodes.label: Regional defense alignment intensity
nodes.description: Degree of formalized military-security cooperation and mutual defence coordination among regional actors, on a continuous scale.

nodes.label: Bargaining pressure in negotiations
nodes.description: Intensity and asymmetry of diplomatic demands, concessions, and coercive leverage shaping negotiations over transit and access.

nodes.label: Leadership hardline cohesion
nodes.description: Degree of ideological cohesion and centralization among domestic political actors favoring uncompromising or confrontational policy stances.

nodes.label: Oil market risk premium
nodes.description: Component of oil prices that reflects compensation demanded by markets for geopolitical, supply-disruption, and security risks.

nodes.label: Futures market volatility
nodes.description: Measured short-term volatility in oil futures and related derivatives markets, indicating uncertainty about future price paths.

nodes.label: Refinery throughput rate
nodes.description: Rate at which refineries process crude into refined products, net of planned and unplanned outages, measured per unit time.

nodes.label: Refined product inventory level
nodes.description: Aggregate onshore and strategic stocks of refined petroleum products (e.g., gasoline, diesel) held in storage across markets.

nodes.label: Tanker insurance premium level
nodes.description: Average insurance and war-risk premium charged for commercial tanker passage through contested or high-risk waters.

nodes.label: Investor risk sentiment
nodes.description: Aggregate market participants' appetite for risk in financial markets sensitive to geopolitical and commodity shocks, reflected in capital flows and asset valuations.

nodes.label: Global oil demand rate
nodes.description: Aggregate rate of oil consumption across global economies measured per unit time, reflecting economic activity and seasonal patterns.

nodes.label: Air-defence capacity
nodes.description: The operational availability and effectiveness of air-defence assets (radar, interceptors, launchers, crews) at a system level.

nodes.label: Interceptor supply resilience
nodes.description: The robustness and replenishment speed of supply chains and inventories for interceptors and counter-drone munitions.

nodes.label: Drone technology diffusion rate
nodes.description: The rate at which drone-related knowledge, designs, software and operational expertise spread among actors and markets.

nodes.label: Unmanned systems production rate
nodes.description: The pace of manufacturing and assembly of unmanned aerial and loitering munitions across legitimate and illicit producers.

nodes.label: Sanctions‑evasion activity
nodes.description: The intensity and effectiveness of logistics, financial and legal methods used to circumvent export controls and sanctions.

nodes.label: Cyberattack frequency
nodes.description: The rate and scale of cyber operations (disruption, espionage, enabling attacks) tied to the hybrid drone campaign.

nodes.label: Cross‑border incident rate
nodes.description: The frequency of incidents that physically or politically cross borders (strikes, airspace violations, spillovers) per unit time.

nodes.label: Critical infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The susceptibility of ports, refineries, logistics nodes and other civilian infrastructure to disruption or damage from attacks.

nodes.label: International security cooperation level
nodes.description: The degree of coordinated policy, intelligence-sharing and joint response capacity among security partners relevant to hybrid threats.

nodes.label: Escalation pressure
nodes.description: The political and operational pressure on actors to respond with stronger measures, retaliation, or widening use of force.

nodes.label: Drone component availability
nodes.description: The market availability and diversity of commercially and militarily relevant drone components and subsystems.

nodes.label: Non‑state operational capacity
nodes.description: The aggregated operational ability of non-state and proxy actors to acquire, operate and sustain unmanned systems and associated operations.

nodes.label: Intelligence‑cyber integration level
nodes.description: The degree to which intelligence, cyber operations and kinetic planning are integrated and coordinated to enable hybrid campaigns.

nodes.label: Public threat perception
nodes.description: The prevailing public and policymaker sense of vulnerability and urgency regarding drone-enabled hybrid threats.

nodes.label: Trade flow disruption
nodes.description: The magnitude and persistence of interruptions to trade and logistics flows (ports, grain, oil, shipping) caused by the conflict system.

nodes.description: Measures the installed and operable production capacity for advanced-manufacturing sectors (semiconductors, batteries, EV components, shipyards) available to meet demand.

nodes.label: Critical materials availability
nodes.description: Measures the accessible supply (stocks, production, and secured imports) of critical minerals and precursor materials used in high‑tech manufacturing.

nodes.label: R&D intensity in high‑tech sectors
nodes.description: Measures the rate of investment and activity in research, development and innovation within technologies relevant to advanced manufacturing.

nodes.label: Trade control and export restriction level
nodes.description: Measures the breadth and strictness of trade controls, export restrictions and licensing regimes affecting technology and inputs.

nodes.label: Industrial subsidy intensity
nodes.description: Measures the magnitude and tempo of government financial support (grants, tax breaks, loans) directed to targeted industrial sectors.

nodes.label: Defense procurement demand
nodes.description: Measures the volume and growth rate of procurement demand originating from defense and security requirements for advanced industrial goods.

nodes.label: Cross‑border capital flows
nodes.description: Measures the net flows of foreign direct investment, portfolio capital and strategic financing into relevant industrial and technology sectors.

nodes.label: Supply‑chain resilience
nodes.description: Measures the system's ability to maintain material, component and information flows and recover from disruptions across value chains.

nodes.label: Logistics chokepoint congestion
nodes.description: Measures the degree of congestion, capacity stress and time delays at critical transport and transshipment nodes that affect trade flows.

nodes.label: Joint‑venture and partnering rate
nodes.description: Measures the frequency and intensity at which firms form cross‑border joint ventures, licensing arrangements and strategic partnerships.

nodes.label: Technology transfer rate
nodes.description: Measures the pace and volume of technology, know‑how and skilled‑labor movements between organizations and across borders.

nodes.label: Manufacturing relocalization rate
nodes.description: Measures the speed and scale at which production footprints are relocated (reshored, near‑shored or diversified) across jurisdictions.

nodes.label: Global demand for clean/high‑tech goods
nodes.description: Measures aggregate market demand dynamics for goods that drive advanced value chains (clean energy technologies, EVs, AI hardware).

nodes.label: Access to advanced equipment
nodes.description: Measures availability and lead times for specialized capital goods and manufacturing tools required for advanced production processes.

nodes.label: Investor risk perception
nodes.description: Measures market and investor perceptions of geopolitical, regulatory and commercial risks affecting willingness to finance industrial projects.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny intensity
nodes.description: Measures the degree and aggressiveness of regulatory review, competition/antitrust oversight and transaction screening in relevant sectors.

nodes.description: The installed output potential of manufacturing sectors measured as producible goods per period given existing plants and equipment.

nodes.label: Advanced technology capability
nodes.description: Cumulative level of high-end technological know‑how, talent, and production capability in domains like microelectronics and AI.

nodes.label: Manufacturing export flow
nodes.description: The rate and volume of outbound shipments of manufactured goods across borders per unit time.

nodes.label: Technology transfer flow
nodes.description: The rate at which technical knowledge, designs, intellectual property, and production techniques move between jurisdictions and firms.

nodes.label: Logistics route diversity
nodes.description: The degree to which supply movements are distributed across multiple maritime, land and air corridors instead of concentrated chokepoints.

nodes.label: Strategic military presence
nodes.description: Scale, disposition and persistence of forward-deployed military assets and force-projection activities in a region.

nodes.label: Defense operations tempo
nodes.description: Frequency and intensity of military exercises, patrols, missile tests and related operational activities over time.

nodes.label: Trade restriction level
nodes.description: Aggregate intensity of export controls, tariffs, licensing rules and formal trade barriers affecting cross-border commerce.

nodes.label: Investment capital flow
nodes.description: Net cross-border flows of equity, debt and direct investment into industrial and technology sectors per unit time.

nodes.label: Capital market accessibility
nodes.description: Ease of access to equity and debt financing across jurisdictions, including listing access and investor openness.

nodes.label: Supply chain resilience
nodes.description: Ability of production systems to maintain output amid disruptions via inventory, substitution, and rerouting mechanisms.

nodes.label: Geopolitical tension perception
nodes.description: Collective perceived level of strategic threat and political friction among states and firms that influences cooperation and risk-taking.

nodes.label: Supplier reorientation rate
nodes.description: Speed at which firms change supplier relationships and relocate production across borders in response to incentives or risks.

nodes.label: Technological ecosystem fragmentation
nodes.description: Degree of divergence between regional technology standards, platforms, and compatible supply chains creating separate ecosystems.

nodes.label: Energy and logistics costs
nodes.description: Aggregate transport fuel, shipping and logistics cost levels that shape the economic viability of supply routes and production locations.

nodes.label: Regulatory harmonization level
nodes.description: Extent of alignment and mutual recognition of standards, certification regimes and regulatory rules across jurisdictions.

Consumer price inflation rate
nodes.description: The ongoing percentage change in a broad consumer price index over a rolling annual or monthly horizon, capturing general price-level inflation.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: The market- and survey-implied anticipated future inflation rate over multiple horizons, reflecting collective expectations about price trends.

nodes.label: Policy interest rate level
nodes.description: The prevailing short-term policy interest rate set or targeted by monetary authorities, forming the baseline for borrowing costs.

nodes.label: Forward guidance signal strength
nodes.description: The intensity and clarity of official communications about future policy intentions, measured by the degree to which guidance shifts market expectations.

nodes.label: Official FX intervention level
nodes.description: The frequency and scale of deliberate official market operations in foreign exchange markets intended to influence exchange rates.

nodes.label: Sovereign yield curve level
nodes.description: The absolute level and slope of sovereign bond yields across maturities, summarizing term structure pricing for risk-free rates.

nodes.label: Bond market liquidity
nodes.description: The depth, bid-ask tightness, and immediacy of execution in sovereign bond markets, indicating how easily positions can be transacted.

nodes.label: Exchange rate levels
nodes.description: The prevailing nominal price levels of major cross-border exchange rates or key bilateral exchange relationships.

nodes.label: Exchange rate volatility
nodes.description: The realized or implied short- to medium-term variability of exchange rates capturing market uncertainty and repricing dynamics.

nodes.label: Cross-border capital flow intensity
nodes.description: The net volume and velocity of capital moving across borders (portfolio, deposit, and funding flows) over a defined period.

nodes.label: Safe-haven commodity price level
nodes.description: The market price level of commodities typically used as liquidity or risk-off stores, reflecting demand for safety assets.

nodes.label: Energy price level
nodes.description: The prevailing price level for energy commodities, representing cost pressures and inflation transmission from energy markets.

nodes.label: Market sentiment and risk appetite
nodes.description: The collective assessment of risk-on versus risk-off positioning expressed through valuations, flows, and derivative indicators.

nodes.label: Investor leverage and positioning
nodes.description: The aggregate degree of leverage, directional exposures, and hedging positions held by investors across asset classes.

nodes.label: Geopolitical tail-risk intensity
nodes.description: The perceived probability and potential severity of low-probability, high-impact geopolitical shocks that could disrupt markets.

nodes.label: Cross-currency funding stress
nodes.description: The degree of stress in FX and cross-currency funding markets as measured by basis spreads, term premia, and funding liquidity strains.

Shipping bottlenecks, port closures and sanctions interrupt exports and transits of ores, specialty gases and precursor chemicals, directly reducing accessible stocks and imports of critical materials.

Persistent interruptions to routes, longer transit times and increased losses strain inventory buffers and logistics redundancy, directly degrading the ability of high‑tech supply chains to maintain flows and recover.

New or expanded advanced-manufacturing capacity in competing Chinese or allied jurisdictions increases global supply and diverts customer orders away from Taiwanese producers, lowering Taiwan's manufactured export volumes over the following production cycles.

Reduced availability of critical inputs lifts producer costs and supply‑side price pressures in manufacturing chains, which markets and surveys quickly translate into higher expected future consumer inflation (and conversely greater availability lowers those expectations).

Tighter export controls and licensing regimes interrupt normal cross-border payments and correspondent-banking relationships and force firms to seek hard-currency pre-funding or alternative corridors, immediately widening basis spreads and reducing FX liquidity.

Sharp, policy-driven trade restrictions create abrupt one-sided FX flows and volatility (eg sudden export/import payment shifts or sanction-triggered flows), prompting monetary authorities to conduct larger or more frequent FX market interventions to stabilize exchange rates.

Rapid expansion of export controls on maritime and dual‑use technology prompts Beijing to respond with more assertive naval/coast‑guard patrols and closer operational coordination with regional partners (including proxy harassment), increasing hostile interdiction and harassment incidents in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

Broader export controls and tightened secondary‑sanctions enforcement raise legal, compliance and insurance risks for shipowners and charterers, causing firms to suspend or reroute tanker transits through Hormuz and temporarily reduce throughput.

Escalating export controls and visible tech‑rivalry confrontations increase market expectations of retaliatory measures or escalation affecting Gulf transit, so traders and risk‑models add a higher geopolitical risk premium to oil prices.

Tighter export controls and licensing on chips, sensors and dual‑use subsystems directly block legal shipments and raise prices/uncertainty for intermediaries supplying the Russia‑Ukraine theatre, reducing the market availability of drone components within weeks.

Stricter export controls incentivize covert routing and use of third‑country brokers for restricted tech transfers, increasing the number of interdictions, seizures and contested transit incidents that cross political or physical borders.

Tighter export controls and licensing (e.g., US/Allied restrictions on chip tools and design IP) impose legal and commercial barriers that directly reduce the legal rate at which Taiwanese firms can transfer advanced designs, tooling, and IP to mainland Chinese partners.

Sustained net inflows into a jurisdiction's tech/industrial sectors relax external financing constraints and currency pressure, reducing the need for monetary authorities to hike policy rates (or allowing them to cut) to stabilize markets and fund the economy.

Increased cross‑border capital into relevant manufacturers or trading intermediaries enables ramped production or bulk purchases of complete UAVs and rapid export to combat actors, raising the frequency of drone strikes as inventories and production are expanded.

A fall in cross-border capital (driven by sanctions, tighter screening, or risk aversion tied to the rivalry) immediately reduces net inbound equity and direct investment from Chinese and third‑party investors into Taiwanese industrial and tech firms.

Improved supply‑chain resilience (alternative qualified suppliers, validated second‑source production and logistics redundancies) directly sustains flows of drone parts and spares into combat zones despite sanctions or interdictions, increasing component availability quickly.

Improved resilience (diversified suppliers, redundant logistics, stockpiles) reduces production interruptions and loss of engineering staff, thereby preserving and modestly enhancing Taiwan's cumulative high‑end technical know‑how and production capability.

Increases in Taiwan's high-end semiconductor and sensor production capacity directly raise the global supply of chips and guidance components that are re‑exported or incorporated into drones used by actors in the Russia–Ukraine theater.

When Taiwanese firms (e.g., leading foundries) increase process-node know‑how and deploy it in existing fabs, they directly raise operable advanced-manufacturing throughput (semiconductor wafer starts and advanced module output) available to global markets.

A sustained rise in Taiwan's manufacturing export shipments increases foreign‑currency (USD) inflows into the region, easing demand for safe‑haven currencies and putting downward pressure on major USD bilateral exchange rates (i.e., USD weakens vs affected Asian currencies).

A sudden fall in Taiwan-origin manufactured exports signals weaker global industrial activity and reduces near-term refinery feedstock and refined-product demand, producing fewer tanker loadings and a measurable drop in transit volume through key chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz.

Sustained high-volume outbound shipments of critical components (chips, modules) from Taiwanese manufacturers directly reduce upstream shortages and bottlenecks, thereby improving the ability of US/China technology value chains to maintain production and recover from disruptions.

An increase in cross‑border technology transfer reduces operational uncertainty for multinationals in supply chains, decreasing precautionary drawdowns of USD credit lines and hedging demand and thereby easing cross‑currency funding strains over time.

Accelerated transfer of guidance algorithms, AI payload designs, or manufacturing know‑how from Taiwan to firms in the region enables faster fielding of more effective UAVs by third parties or beneficiaries, raising the frequency and effectiveness of drone attacks in the Russia–Ukraine war.

An uptick in transfers of sensitive designs, process IP or equipment from Taiwanese entities to PRC firms triggers immediate policy responses (licensing changes, new entity listings and stricter export controls) from the US and allies to block further leakage.

An abrupt increase in export controls or licensing on Taiwan tech and components forces corporates and suppliers to pre-fund imports and roll or extend USD hedges, sharply raising demand for dollar liquidity and widening cross‑currency basis spreads.

Escalation of export controls on Taiwanese tech provokes PRC coercive signaling and forward naval/paramilitary deployments as deterrence and bargaining leverage, which increases harassment, interdiction attempts and close encounters by forces operating in distant but politically salient sea lanes including the Strait of Hormuz.

Tighter export controls or licensing restrictions on Taiwanese-origin advanced components and related tooling reduce the channels through which those parts reach intermediaries and end users, lowering the pool of drone components available to participants in the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

Larger net inbound investment capital into Taiwan reduces bilateral capital‑flight and depreciation pressure on regional currencies, lowering the frequency and scale of official FX intervention by regional central banks seeking to defend exchange rates.

Increased cross‑border investment into Taiwanese and regional subcontractors expands manufacturing capacity and inventories for drone subsystems, which after lead times become available to global markets that can supply the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

Increases in cross‑border investment originating in or routed through Taiwanese firms (e.g., project finance, JV capital for fabs abroad) directly raise measurable cross‑border capital flows into PRC or regional technology sectors involved in the US–China rivalry.

Rising inflation expectations increase macroeconomic and policy uncertainty and boost hedging and precautionary demand, prompting market participants to price a larger geopolitical/supply risk component into oil (higher oil risk premium).
Tighter policy interest rates in major economies raise borrowing costs and damp aggregate demand and commodity financing, reducing near‑term oil consumption and lowering spot crude prices.

Higher global policy interest rates increase home‑market returns and discount rates while raising borrowing costs for leveraged cross‑border deals, directly reducing appetite and feasibility for foreign portfolio and direct investment into Taiwanese industry and tech.

Sustained increases in major policy rates raise global borrowing costs and compress venture and project returns, prompting investors and banks to scale back cross‑border financing for capital‑intensive advanced‑manufacturing and semiconductor investments linked to US–China competition.

Frequent or large official FX interventions are often accompanied by tighter FX monitoring and controls (capital‑flow management) that directly complicate cross‑border payments, royalties and joint‑venture funding, prompting firms to scale back or slow formal technology licensing and co‑development agreements with Taiwanese partners.

Large or highly visible official FX interventions (e.g., persistent currency defense or managed depreciation) are perceived as competitive economic measures and tend to trigger reciprocal political and regulatory responses, including tighter export controls and licensing on sensitive technologies.

A materially stronger reserve currency (e.g., USD) increases the real purchasing power of US/allied defence and security budgets for forward deployments and escorts, sustaining patrol presence in the Strait and lowering the frequency of hostile or interdiction incidents.

A depreciation of the ruble (a rise in the ruble‑per‑USD exchange rate) raises the local currency price of imported drone parts, reducing procurement volumes and diversity of foreign suppliers for components.

A stronger foreign currency (e.g., USD appreciation / higher USD/TWD exchange rate) makes Taiwan's USD‑priced manufactured goods cheaper for buyers abroad, directly raising export volumes as exporters win or expand orders and pass through price competitiveness.

Sharp adverse moves in bilateral exchange rates (an importer’s currency weakening) raise the local‑currency cost of imported critical minerals and precursors, causing buyers to curtail orders and suppliers to reallocate stock, reducing near‑term availability for high‑tech manufacturing.

Acute cross‑currency funding stress raises dollar/working‑capital costs for shipowners, charterers and insurers, causing cancellations, delays or rerouting of tanker voyages and thereby reducing tanker transit volumes through Hormuz.

Rising cross‑currency funding stress increases the cost and reduces the availability of foreign‑currency payments for Russian importers and third‑party intermediaries, choking off purchases of foreign drone components and subsystems.

Elevated cross‑currency funding stress raises the cost and availability constraints of dollar and other foreign funding for Taiwanese firms and foreign investors, causing immediate reductions or delays in cross‑border equity, debt and project finance into Taiwan.

Spikes in cross‑currency funding stress raise hedging costs and cut dollar liquidity for overseas borrowers and investors, forcing suspension or cancellation of FDI, portfolio flows and project financing into tech and industrial projects tied to the US–China rivalry.
